parakeet: The danger is not just that Christianity can justify harm, it's that Christianity is diverse enough to deny responsibility for the harm it keeps helping create. Christianity's cherry-picking problem makes the religion harder to confront because it allows Christianity to be both harmful and evasive at the same time. It can produce harm through one framework and moral camouflage through another. It can dominate politically through one wing and seem harmless through another. It can claim timeless truth while constantly rearranging its emphasis to survive critique. So for someone trying to reduce Christianity's public influence, the task cannot just be prove this doctrine is bad or expose this denomination as harmful. The stronger move is to expose the larger pattern. Christianity repeatedly turns selective interpretation into moral authority and then uses its internal diversity to avoid full accountability for the social consequences. Christianity is a tradition flexible enough to generate contradictory moral worlds, yet confident enough to seek public authority as though it speaks with one divine voice. In practice, this means critics should probably focus less on proving that all Christianity is identical, and more on showing how often harmful outcomes recur across different expressions, how divine authority amplifies selective moral claims, how theological flexibility helps Christianity survive criticism, and why no religion that fragmented should wield outsized power over public life. Christianity's cherry-picking problem does not just make the religion inconsistent, it makes it politically slippery and sloppy. Every time you expose one harmful expression, another expression appears to absorb the critique, protect the brand, and preserve the institution's legitimacy in public life. The danger is not just that Christianity can justify harm, it's that Christianity is diverse enough to deny responsibility for the harm it keeps helping create. Christianity is not just winning through doctrine, it's winning through formation, familiarity, symbolism, and infrastructure. If humanists want to make a dent, they have to build something people can actually belong to, not just something they can agree with. You cannot outlawyer a religion that is out-parenting, outstorytelling, out-symbolizing, and outorganizing you by leaps and bounds. Humanism has to be more than a reaction, it has to evolve into a place to stand and a way forward.
